senses.d: Not used; not habituated; unfamiliar; unused; — with to.
q: Chastened as a bullock unaccustomed to the yoke.

senses.d: Not usual; uncommon; strange; new.
q: What unaccustomed cause procures her hither?

senses.d: Not prudent; not discreet; ill advised.
Done without due consideration; wanton; rash; inconsiderate; as, an unadvised proceeding.
Not aware; not noticing; giving no heed; thoughtless; inattentive.
Unawares.
Without design or preparation; suddenly; without premeditation, unexpectedly.
q: Lest unawares we lose This our high place, our sanctuary, our hill.

senses.d: The withholding of belief; doubt; incredulity; skepticism.
Disbelief; especially, disbelief of divine revelation, or in a divine providence or scheme of redemption.
q: Blind unbelief is sure to err, And scan his work in vain.

Unbelief.etym: [Pref. un- not + belief: cf. AS. ungeleáfa.]

senses.d: One who does not believe; an incredulous person; a doubter; a skeptic.
A disbeliever; especially, one who does not believe that the Bible is a divine revelation, and holds that Christ was neither a divine nor a supernatural person; an infidel; a freethinker.
Not believing; incredulous; doubting; distrusting; skeptical.
Believing the thing alleged not to be true; disbelieving; especially, believing that the Bible is not a divine revelation, or that Christ was not a divine or a supernatural person.
Not certain; not having certain knowledge; not assured in mind; distrustful.
q: Man, without the protection of a superior Being, . . . is uncertain of everything that he hopes for.

senses.d: Irresolute; inconsonant; variable; untrustworthy; as, an uncertain person; an uncertain breeze.
q: O woman! in our hours of ease, Uncertain, coy, and hard to please!

senses.d: Questionable; equivocal; indefinite; problematical.
q: From certain dangers to uncertain praise.

senses.d: Not sure; liable to fall or err; fallible.
q: Soon bent his bow, uncertain in his aim.
Whistling slings dismissed the uncertain stone.

senses.d: To make uncertain.

Uncertain.etym: [1st pref. un- + certain; or fr. uncertain, a.]

senses.d: In an uncertain manner.
Not circumcised; hence, not of the Israelites.
The absence or want of circumcision.
People not circumcised; the Gentiles.
The brother of one's father or mother; also applied to an aunt's husband; — the correlative of aunt in sex, and of nephew and niece in relationship.
A pawnbroker.

Uncle.etym: [OE. uncle, OF. oncle, uncle, F. oncle, fr. L. avunculus a maternal uncle, dim. of avus a grandfather; akin to Lith. avynas uncle, Goth. aw� grandmother, Icel. āi great grandfather.]

senses.d: An eldery man; — used chiefly as a kindly or familiar appellation, esp. (Southern U. S.) for a worthy old negro; as, “Uncle Remus.”
q: Plain old uncle as he was, with his great ears, — an immense talker.

senses.d: Not clean; foul; dirty; filthy.
Ceremonially impure; needing ritual cleansing.
q: He that toucheth the dead body of any man shall be unclean seven days.

senses.d: Morally impure.
To strip of clothes or covering; to make naked.
q: do groan being burdened; not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon.

senses.d: Divested or stripped of clothing.
Not yet clothed; wanting clothes; naked.
Not comely.
In an uncomely manner.
Incorrupt.
Incorruptible.
To take the cover from; to divest of covering; as, to uncover a box, bed, house, or the like; to uncover one's body.
To show openly; to disclose; to reveal.
To divest of the hat or cap; to bare the head of; as, to uncover one's head; to uncover one's self.
To take off the hat or cap; to bare the head in token of respect.
q: We are forced to uncover after them.

senses.d: To remove the covers from dishes, or the like.
q: Uncover, dogs, and lap.

senses.d: The act of anointing, smearing, or rubbing with an unguent, oil, or ointment, especially for medical purposes, or as a symbol of consecration; as, mercurial unction.
q: To be heir, and to be king By sacred unction, thy deserved right.

senses.d: That which is used for anointing; an unguent; an ointment; hence, anything soothing or lenitive.
q: The king himself the sacred unction made.
Lay not that flattering unction to your soul.

senses.d: Divine or sanctifying grace.
That quality in language, address, or the like, which excites emotion; especially, strong devotion; religious fervor and tenderness; sometimes, a simulated, factitious, or unnatural fervor.
q: The delightful equivoque and unction of the passage in Farquhar.
The mention of thy glory Is unction to the breast.

Unction.etym: [OE. unccioun, uncioun, OF. oncion, onction, F. onction, fr. L. unctio, fr. ungere, unctum, to anoint. See Unguent.]

senses.d: Below or lower, in place or position, with the idea of being covered; lower than; beneath; — opposed to over; as, he stood under a tree; the carriage is under cover; a cellar extends under the whole house.
q: Fruit put in bottles, and the bottles let down into wells under water, will keep long.
Be gathered now, ye waters under heaven, Into one place.

senses.d: Denoting relation to some thing or person that is superior, weighs upon, oppresses, bows down, governs, directs, influences powerfully, or the like, in a relation of subjection, subordination, obligation, liability, or the like; as, to travel under a heavy load; to live under extreme oppression; to have fortitude under the evils of life; to have patience under pain, or under misfortunes; to behave like a Christian under reproaches and injuries; under the pains and penalties of the law; the condition under which one enters upon an office; under the necessity of obeying the laws; under vows of chastity.
q: Both Jews and Gentiles . . . are all under sin.
That led the embattled seraphim to war Under thy conduct.
Who have their provand Only for bearing burdens, and sore blows For sinking under them.

senses.d: Denoting relation to something that exceeds in rank or degree, in number, size, weight, age, or the like; in a relation of the less to the greater, of inferiority, or of falling short.
q: Three sons he dying left under age.
Medicines take effect sometimes under, and sometimes above, the natural proportion of their virtue.
There are several hundred parishes in England under twenty pounds a year.
It was too great an honor for any man under a duke.
Several young men could never leave the pulpit under half a dozen conceits.

senses.d: Denoting relation to something that comprehends or includes, that represents or designates, that furnishes a cover, pretext, pretense, or the like; as, he betrayed him under the guise of friendship; Morpheus is represented under the figure of a boy asleep.
q: A crew who, under names of old renown . . . abused Fanatic Egypt.
Mr. Duke may be mentioned under the double capacity of a poet and a divine.
Under this head may come in the several contests and wars betwixt popes and the secular princes.

senses.d: Less specifically, denoting the relation of being subject, of undergoing regard, treatment, or the like; as, a bill under discussion.
q: Abject and lost, lay these, covering the flood, Under amazement of their hideous change.

Under.etym: [AS. under, prep. & adv.; akin to OFries. under, OS. undar, D. onder, G. unter, OHG. untar, Icel. undir, Sw. & Dan. under, Goth. undar, L. infra below, inferior lower, Skr. adhas below. √201. Cf. Inferior.]

senses.d: In a lower, subject, or subordinate condition; in subjection; — used chiefly in a few idiomatic phrases; as, to bring under, to reduce to subjection; to subdue; to keep under, to keep in subjection; to control; to go under, to be unsuccessful; to fail.
q: I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection.
The minstrel fell, but the foeman's chain Could not bring his proud soul under.

senses.d: Lower in position, intensity, rank, or degree; subject; subordinate; — generally in composition with a noun, and written with or without the hyphen; as, an undercurrent; undertone; underdose; under-garment; underofficer; undersheriff.
To bind below; to gird round the bottom.
q: They used helps, undergirding the ship.

senses.d: Beneath; below; in a lower place; under; as, a channel underneath the soil.
q: Or sullen mole, that runneth underneath.

senses.d: Under; beneath; below.
q: Underneath this stone lie As much beauty as could die.

senses.d: One who, or that which, undersets or supports; a prop; a support; a pedestal.

To have just and adequate ideas of; to apprehended the meaning or intention of; to have knowledge of; to comprehend; to know; as, to understand a problem in Euclid; to understand a proposition or a declaration; the court understands the advocate or his argument; to understand the sacred oracles; to understand a nod or a wink.
q: Speaketh [i.e., speak thou] so plain at this time, I you pray, That we may understande what ye say.
I understand not what you mean by this.
Understood not all was but a show.
A tongue not understanded of the people.

senses.d: To be apprised, or have information, of; to learn; to be informed of; to hear; as, I understand that Congress has passed the bill.
To recognize or hold as being or signifying; to suppose to mean; to interpret; to explain.
q: The most learned interpreters understood the words of sin, and not of Abel.

senses.d: To mean without expressing; to imply tacitly; to take for granted; to assume.
q: War, then, war, Open or understood, must be resolved.

senses.d: To stand under; to support.

Understand.etym: [OE. understanden, AS. understandan, literally, to stand under; cf. AS. forstandan to understand, G. verstehen. The development of sense is not clear. See Under, and Stand.]

senses.d: To have the use of the intellectual faculties; to be an intelligent being.
q: Imparadised in you, in whom alone I understand, and grow, and see.

senses.d: To be informed; to have or receive knowledge.
q: I came to Jerusalem, and understood of the evil that Eliashib did for Tobiah.

senses.d: Knowing; intelligent; skillful; as, he is an understanding man.
The act of one who understands a thing, in any sense of the verb; knowledge; discernment; comprehension; interpretation; explanation.
An agreement of opinion or feeling; adjustment of differences; harmony; anything mutually understood or agreed upon; as, to come to an understanding with another.
q: He hoped the loyalty of his subjects would concur with him in the preserving of a good understanding between him and his people.

senses.d: The power to understand; the intellectual faculty; the intelligence; the rational powers collectively conceived an designated; the higher capacities of the intellect; the power to distinguish truth from falsehood, and to adapt means to ends.
q: There is a spirit in man; and the inspiration of the Almighty them understanding.

The power of perception is that which we call the understanding. Perception, which we make the act of the understanding, is of three sorts: 1. The perception of ideas in our mind; 2. The perception of the signification of signs; 3. The perception of the connection or repugnancy, agreement or disagreement, that there is between any of our ideas. All these are attributed to the understanding, or perceptive power, though it be the two latter only that use allows us to say we understand.

In its wider acceptation, understanding is the entire power of perceiving an conceiving, exclusive of the sensibility: the power of dealing with the impressions of sense, and composing them into wholes, according to a law of unity; and in its most comprehensive meaning it includes even simple apprehension.

senses.d: Specifically, the discursive faculty; the faculty of knowing by the medium or use of general conceptions or relations. In this sense it is contrasted with, and distinguished from, the reason.
q: I use the term understanding, not for the noetic faculty, intellect proper, or place of principles, but for the dianoetic or discursive faculty in its widest signification, for the faculty of relations or comparisons; and thus in the meaning in which “verstand” is now employed by the Germans.

senses.d: To take upon one's self; to engage in; to enter upon; to take in hand; to begin to perform; to set about; to attempt.
q: To second, or oppose, or undertake The perilous attempt.

senses.d: Specifically, to take upon one's self solemnly or expressly; to lay one's self under obligation, or to enter into stipulations, to perform or to execute; to covenant; to contract.
q: I 'll undertake to land them on our coast.

senses.d: Hence, to guarantee; to promise; to affirm.
q: And he was not right fat, I undertake.
And those two counties I will undertake Your grace shall well and quietly enjoiy.
I dare undertake they will not lose their labor.

senses.d: To assume, as a character.
To engage with; to attack.
q: It is not fit your lordship should undertake every companion that you give offense to.

senses.d: To have knowledge of; to hear.
To take or have the charge of.
q: Keep well those that ye undertake.

senses.d: To take upon one's self, or assume, any business, duty, or province.
q: O Lord, I am oppressed; undertake for me.

senses.d: To venture; to hazard.
q: It is the cowish terror of his spirit That dare not undertake.

senses.d: To give a promise or guarantee; to be surety.
q: But on mine honor dare I undertake For good lord Titus' innocence in all.

senses.d: To reverse, as what has been done; to annul; to bring to naught.
q: What's done can not be undone.
To-morrow, ere the setting sun, She 'd all undo that she had done.

senses.d: To loose; to open; to take to piece; to unfasten; to untie; hence, to unravel; to solve; as, to undo a knot; to undo a puzzling question; to undo a riddle.
q: Pray you, undo this button.
She took the spindle, and undoing the thread gradually, measured it.

senses.d: To bring to poverty; to impoverish; to ruin, as in reputation, morals, hopes, or the like; as, many are undone by unavoidable losses, but more undo themselves by vices and dissipation, or by indolence.
q: That quaffing and drinking will undo you,

Undo.etym: [AS. und�n. See 1st Un-, and Do to perform.]

senses.d: Not done or performed; neglected.
To divest of clothes; to strip.
To divest of ornaments to disrobe.
To take the dressing, or covering, from; as, to undress a wound.
A loose, negligent dress; ordinary dress, as distinguished from full dress.
An authorized habitual dress of officers and soldiers, but not full-dress uniform.

Not equal; not matched; not of the same size, length, breadth, quantity, strength, talents, acquirements, age, station, or the like; as, the fingers are of unequal length; peers and commoners are unequal in rank.
Ill balanced or matched; disproportioned; hence, not equitable; partial; unjust; unfair.
q: Against unequal arms to fight in pain.
Jerome, a very unequal relator of the opinion of his adversaries.
To punish me for what you make me do Seems much unequal.

senses.d: Not uniform; not equable; irregular; uneven; as, unequal pulsations; an unequal poem.
Not adequate or sufficient; inferior; as, the man was unequal to the emergency; the timber was unequal to the sudden strain.
Not having the two sides or the parts symmetrical.
In an unequal manner.
Not faithful; not observant of promises, vows, allegiance, or duty; violating trust or confidence; treacherous; perfidious; as, an unfaithful subject; an unfaithful agent or servant.
q: My feet, through wine, unfaithful to their weight.
His honor rooted in dishonor stood, And faith unfaithful kept him falsely true.

senses.d: Not possessing faith; infidel.
Not feigned; not counterfeit; not hypocritical; real; sincere; genuine; as, unfeigned piety; unfeigned love to man.
Not producing fruit or offspring; unproductive; infertile; barren; sterile; as, an unfruitful tree or animal; unfruitful soil; an unfruitful life or effort.
To loose the girdle or band of; to unbind; to unload.
q: He ungirded his camels.

senses.d: To deprive of divinity; to undeify.
To cause to recognize no god; to deprive of a god; to make atheistical.
Not godly; not having regard for God; disobedient to God; wicked; impious; sinful.
Polluted by sin or wickedness.
q: The hours of this ungodly day.

senses.d: Not holy; unhallowed; not consecrated; hence, profane; wicked; impious.
A fabulous animal with one horn; the monoceros; — often represented in heraldry as a supporter.
A two-horned animal of some unknown kind, so called in the Authorized Version of the Scriptures.
q: Canst thou bind the unicorn with his band in the furrow?

senses.d: Any large beetle having a hornlike prominence on the head or prothorax.
The kamichi; — called also unicorn bird.
A howitzer.

Unicorn.etym: [OE. unicorne, F. unicorne, L. unicornis one-horned, having a single horn; unus one + cornu a horn; cf. L. unicornuus a unicorn. See One, and Horn.]

senses.d: A single thing or person.
The least whole number; one.
q: Units are the integral parts of any large number.

senses.d: A gold coin of the reign of James I., of the value of twenty shillings.
Any determinate amount or quantity (as of length, time, heat, value) adopted as a standard of measurement for other amounts or quantities of the same kind.
A single thing, as a magnitude or number, regarded as an undivided whole.

To put together so as to make one; to join, as two or more constituents, to form a whole; to combine; to connect; to join; to cause to adhere; as, to unite bricks by mortar; to unite iron bars by welding; to unite two armies.

Hence, to join by a legal or moral bond, as families by marriage, nations by treaty, men by opinions; to join in interest, affection, fellowship, or the like; to cause to agree; to harmonize; to associate; to attach.
q: Under his great vicegerent reign abide, United as one individual soul.
The king proposed nothing more than to unite his kingdom in one form of worship.

Unite.syn: To add; join; annex; attach. See Add.
Unite.etym: [L. unitus, p. p. of unire to unite, from unus one. See One.]

senses.d: To become one; to be cemented or consolidated; to combine, as by adhesion or mixture; to coalesce; to grow together.
To join in an act; to concur; to act in concert; as, all parties united in signing the petition.
United; joint; as, unite consent.

Unite.etym: [L. unitus, p. p. See Unite, v. t.]

senses.d: Combined; joined; made one.
The state of being one; oneness.
q: Whatever we can consider as one thing suggests to the understanding the idea of unity.

senses.d: Concord; harmony; conjunction; agreement; uniformity; as, a unity of proofs; unity of doctrine.
q: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!

senses.d: Any definite quantity, or aggregate of quantities or magnitudes taken as one, or for which 1 is made to stand in calculation; thus, in a table of natural sines, the radius of the circle is regarded as unity.

In dramatic composition, one of the principles by which a uniform tenor of story and propriety of representation are preserved; conformity in a composition to these; in oratory, discourse, etc., the due subordination and reference of every part to the development of the leading idea or the eastablishment of the main proposition.
Such a combination of parts as to constitute a whole, or a kind of symmetry of style and character.
The peculiar characteristics of an estate held by several in joint tenancy.

Unity.syn: Union; oneness; junction; concord; harmony. See Union.
Unity.etym: [OE. unite, F. unité, L. unitas, from unus one. See One, and cf. Unit.]

senses.d: Acting contrary to the standard of right; not animated or controlled by justice; false; dishonest; as, an unjust man or judge.
Contrary to justice and right; prompted by a spirit of injustice; wrongful; as, an unjust sentence; an unjust demand; an unjust accusation.
Not known; not apprehended.
To take the load from; to take out the cargo of; as, to unlade a ship or a wagon.
q: The venturous merchant . . . Shall here unlade him and depart no more.

senses.d: To unload; to remove, or to have removed, as a load or a burden; to discharge.
q: There the ship was to unlade her burden.

senses.d: Not lawful; contrary to law.
To forget, as what has been learned; to lose from memory; also, to learn the contrary of.
q: I had learned nothing right; I had to unlearn everything.

senses.d: To fail to learn.
Not learned; untaught; uneducated; ignorant; illiterate.
Not gained by study; not known.
Not exhibiting learning; as, unlearned verses.
Not leavened; containing no leaven; as, unleavened bread.

Upon any less condition than (the fact or thing stated in the sentence or clause which follows); if not; supposing that not; if it be not; were it not that; except; as, we shall fail unless we are industrious.
q: Here nothing breeds unless the nightly owl.

Unless.etym: [Formerly, onles, onlesse, onlesse that, that is, in less, in a less case. See On, and Less.]

senses.d: To make loose; to loosen; to set free.
To become unfastened; to lose all connection or union.
To annul the marriage of; to divorce.
Not merciful; indisposed to mercy or grace; cruel; inhuman; merciless; unkind.
To mar or destroy the perfection of.
Imperfect.
Not reasonable; irrational; immoderate; exorbitant.
Not righteous; evil; wicked; sinful; as, an unrighteous man.
Contrary to law and equity; unjust; as, an unrighteous decree or sentence.

Unrighteous.etym: [OE. unrightwise, AS. unrihtwīs. See Un- not, and Righteous.]

senses.d: Not ripe; as, unripe fruit.
Developing too early; premature.
Not submissive to rule; disregarding restraint; disposed to violate; turbulent; ungovernable; refractory; as, an unruly boy; unruly boy; unruly conduct.
q: But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison.

senses.d: Insatiable.
Not searchable; inscrutable; hidden; mysterious.
q: The counsels of God are to us unsearchable.

senses.d: Not to seem.
Not seemly; unbecoming; indecent.
q: An unseemly outbreak of temper.

senses.d: In an unseemly manner.
Not speakable; incapable of being uttered or adequately described; inexpressible; unutterable; ineffable; as, unspeakable grief or rage.
q: Ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory.

senses.d: Not spotted; free from spot or stain; especially, free from moral stain; unblemished; immaculate; as, an unspotted reputation.
Not stable; not firm, fixed, or constant; subject to change or overthrow.
To take the stopple or stopper from; as, to unstop a bottle or a cask.
To free from any obstruction; to open.
To deprive of temper, or of the proper degree of temper; to make soft.
To; unto; towards; — used of material objects.
q: Taverners until them told the same.
He roused himself full blithe, and hastened them until.

senses.d: To; up to; till; before; — used of time; as, he staid until evening; he will not come back until the end of the month.
q: He and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity.

Until.etym: [OE. until, ontil; un- (as in unto) + til till; cf. Dan. indtil, Sw. intill. See Unto, and Till, prep.]

senses.d: As far as; to the place or degree that; especially, up to the time that; till. See Till, conj.
q: In open prospect nothing bounds our eye, Until the earth seems joined unto the sky.
But the rest of the dead lives not again until the thousand years were finished.

senses.d: An unseasonable time.
q: A man shall not eat in untime.

senses.d: Not timely; done or happening at an unnatural, unusual, or improper time; unseasonable; premature; inopportune; as, untimely frosts; untimely remarks; an untimely death.
Out of the natural or usual time; inopportunely; prematurely; unseasonably.
To; — now used only in antiquated, formal, or scriptural style. See To.
Until; till.

Unto.etym: [OE. unto; un- (only in unto, until) unto, as far as + to to; this un- is akin to AS. �� until, OFries. und OS. und until, conj. (cf. OS. unt� unto, OHG. unzi), Goth. und unto, until. See To, and cf. Until.]

senses.d: Until; till.
Toward.
Froward; perverse.
Awkward; ungraceful.
Inconvenient; troublesome; vexatious; unlucky; unfortunate; as, an untoward wind or accident.
Not washed.
Not weighed; not pondered or considered; as, an unweighed statement.
Not wise; defective in wisdom; injudicious; indiscreet; foolish; as, an unwise man; unwise kings; unwise measures.

Unwise.etym: [AS. unwīs. See Un- not, and Wise, a.]

senses.d: Not knowing; unconscious; ignorant.
Not worthy; wanting merit, value, or fitness; undeserving; worthless; unbecoming; — often with of.
Aloft; on high; in a direction contrary to that of gravity; toward or in a higher place or position; above; — the opposite of down.
q: But up or down, By center or eccentric, hard to tell.

senses.d: From a lower to a higher position, literally or figuratively; as, from a recumbent or sitting position; from the mouth, toward the source, of a river; from a dependent or inferior condition; from concealment; from younger age; from a quiet state, or the like; — used with verbs of motion expressed or implied.
q: But they presumed to go up unto the hilltop.
I am afflicted and ready to die from my youth up.
Up rose the sun, and up rose Emelye.
We have wrought ourselves up into this degree of Christian indifference.

senses.d: In a higher place or position, literally or figuratively; in the state of having arisen; in an upright, or nearly upright, position; standing; mounted on a horse; in a condition of elevation, prominence, advance, proficiency, excitement, insurrection, or the like; — used with verbs of rest, situation, condition, and the like; as, to be up on a hill; the lid of the box was up; prices are up.
q: And when the sun was up, they were scorched.
Those that were up themselves kept others low.
Helen was up — was she?
Rebels there are up, And put the Englishmen unto the sword.
His name was up through all the adjoining provinces, even to Italy and Rome; many desiring to see who he was that could withstand so many years the Roman puissance.
Thou hast fired me; my soul's up in arms.
Grief and passion are like floods raised in little brooks by a sudden rain; they are quickly up.
A general whisper ran among the country people, that Sir Roger was up.
Let us, then, be up and doing, With a heart for any fate.

senses.d: To or in a position of equal advance or equality; not short of, back of, less advanced than, away from, or the like; — usually followed by to or with; as, to be up to the chin in water; to come up with one's companions; to come up with the enemy; to live up to engagements.
q: As a boar was whetting his teeth, up comes a fox to him.

senses.d: To or in a state of completion; completely; wholly; quite; as, in the phrases to eat up; to drink up; to burn up; to sum up; etc.; to shut up the eyes or the mouth; to sew up a rent.
Aside, so as not to be in use; as, to lay up riches; put up your weapons.
q: Up, up, my friend! and quit your books, Or surely you 'll grow double.
Fortune . . . led him up and down.

senses.d: Vertical; perpendicular; — said of the cable when the anchor is under, or nearly under, the hawse hole, and the cable is taut.
the order given to move the tiller toward the upper, or windward, side of a vessel.
What is going on?

Up.etym: [AS. up, upp, �p; akin to OFries. up, op, D. op, OS. �p, OHG. �f, G. auf, Icel. � Sw. upp, Dan. op, Goth. iup, and probably to E. over. See Over.]

senses.d: From a lower to a higher place on, upon, or along; at a higher situation upon; at the top of.
q: In going up a hill, the knees will be most weary; in going down, the thihgs.

senses.d: From the coast towards the interior of, as a country; from the mouth towards the source of, as a stream; as, to journey up the country; to sail up the Hudson.
Upon.
The state of being up or above; a state of elevation, prosperity, or the like; — rarely occurring except in the phrase ups and downs.
q: They had their ups and downs of fortune.

senses.d: Inclining up; tending or going up; upward; as, an up look; an up grade; the up train.
To charge with something wrong or disgraceful; to reproach; to cast something in the teeth of; — followed by with or for, and formerly of, before the thing imputed.
q: And upbraided them with their unbelief.
Vet do not Upbraid us our distress.

senses.d: To reprove severely; to rebuke; to chide.
q: Then began he to upbraid the cities wherein most of his mighty works were done.
How much doth thy kindness upbraid my wickedness!

senses.d: To treat with contempt.
To object or urge as a matter of reproach; to cast up; — with to before the person.

Upbraid.etym: [OE. upbreiden; AS, upp up + bregdan to draw, twist, weave, or the kindred Icel. bregða to draw, brandish, braid, deviate from, change, break off, upbraid. See Up, and Braid, v. t.]

senses.d: To utter upbraidings.
The act of reproaching; contumely.
To hold up; to lift on high; to elevate.
q: The mournful train with groans, and hands upheld. Besought his pity.

senses.d: To keep erect; to support; to sustain; to keep from falling; to maintain.
q: Honor shall uphold the humble in spirit.
Faulconbridge, In spite of spite, alone upholds the day.

senses.d: To aid by approval or encouragement; to countenance; as, to uphold a person in wrongdoing.
On; — used in all the senses of that word, with which it is interchangeable.
q: Our host upon his stirrups stood anon.
Thou shalt take of the blood that is upon the altar.
The Philistines be upon thee, Samson.
As I did stand my watch upon the hill.
He made a great difference between people that did rebel upon wantonness, and them that did rebel upon want.
This advantage we lost upon the invention of firearms.
Upon the whole, it will be necessary to avoid that perpetual repetition of the same epithets which we find in Homer.
He had abandoned the frontiers, retiring upon Glasgow.
Philip swore upon the Evangelists to abstain from aggression in my absence.

Upon.etym: [AS. uppan, uppon; upp up + on, an, on. See Up, and On.]

senses.d: Being further up, literally or figuratively; higher in place, position, rank, dignity, or the like; superior; as, the upper lip; the upper side of a thing; the upper house of a legislature.
The upper leather for a shoe; a vamp.
Highest in place, position, rank, power, or the like; upmost; supreme.
q: Whatever faction happens to be uppermost.

Uppermost.etym: [From Up, Upper; formed like aftermost. Cf. Upmost.]

senses.d: In an erect position or posture; perpendicular; vertical, or nearly vertical; pointing upward; as, an upright tree.
q: With chattering teeth, and bristling hair upright.
All have their ears upright.

senses.d: Morally erect; having rectitude; honest; just; as, a man upright in all his ways.
q: And that man was perfect and upright.

senses.d: Conformable to moral rectitude.
q: Conscience rewards upright conduct with pleasure.

senses.d: Stretched out face upward; flat on the back.

Upright.etym: [AS. upright, uppriht. See Up, and Right, a.]

senses.d: Something standing upright, as a piece of timber in a building. See Illust. of Frame.
Designating a club in which the head is approximately at a right angle with the shaft.

A tool made from a flat strip of steel with chisel edges at both ends, bent into horseshoe, the opening between the cutting edges being adjustable, used for reducing splits to skeins. Called in full upright shave.
In an upright manner.
the quality or state of being upright.
To rise; to get up; to appear from below the horizon.
q: Uprose the virgin with the morning light.

senses.d: To have an upward direction or inclination.
q: Uprose the mystic mountain range.

senses.d: The act of rising; appearance above the horizon; rising.
q: Did ever raven sing so like a lark, That gives sweet tidings of the sun's uprise?

senses.d: Act of rising; also, a steep place; an ascent.
An insurrection; a popular revolt.
Great tumult; violent disturbance and noise; noisy confusion; bustle and clamor.
q: But the Jews which believed not, . . . set all the city on an uproar.

Uproar.etym: [D. oproer; akin to G. aufruhr, Dan. oprör, Sw. uppror; D. op up + roeren to stir; akin to AS. hr�ran to stir, hr�r stirring, active, G. rühren to stir, OHG. ruoren, Icel. hræra, Dan. röre, Sw. röra. Cf. Rearmouse.]

senses.d: To throw into uproar or confusion.
To make an uproar.
The upper side; the part that is uppermost.
q: These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also.

senses.d: In a direction from lower to higher; toward a higher place; in a course toward the source or origin; — opposed to downward; as, to tend or roll upward.
q: Looking inward, we are stricken dumb; looking upward, we speak and prevail.

senses.d: In the upper parts; above.
q: Dagon his name, sea monster, upward man, And down ward fish.

senses.d: Yet more; indefinitely more; above; over.
q: From twenty years old and upward.
I have been your wife in this obedience Upward of twenty years.

senses.d: Directed toward a higher place; as, with upward eye; with upward course.
The upper part; the top.
q: From the extremest upward of thy head.

senses.d: The urus.
Courteous in manners; polite; refined; elegant.
To press; to push; to drive; to impel; to force onward.
q: Through the thick deserts headlong urged his flight.

senses.d: To press the mind or will of; to ply with motives, arguments, persuasion, or importunity.
q: My brother never Did urge me in his act; I did inquire it.

senses.d: To provoke; to exasperate.
q: Urge not my father's anger.

senses.d: To press hard upon; to follow closely
q: Heir urges heir, like wave impelling wave.

senses.d: To present in an urgent manner; to press upon attention; to insist upon; as, to urge an argument; to urge the necessity of a case.
To treat with forcible means; to take severe or violent measures with; as, to urge an ore with intense heat.

Urge.syn: To animate; incite; impel; instigate; stimulate; encourage.
Urge.etym: [L. urgere; akin to E. wreak. See Wreak, v. t.]

senses.d: To press onward or forward.
To be pressing in argument; to insist; to persist.
Urging; pressing; besetting; plying, with importunity; calling for immediate attention; instantly important.
q: Some urgent cause to ordain the contrary.
The Egyptians were urgent upon the people that they might send them out of the land in haste.

Urgent.etym: [L. urgens, p. pr. of urgere: cf. F. urgent. See Urge.]

senses.d: A part or decoration of the breastplate of the high priest among the ancient Jews, by which Jehovah revealed his will on certain occasions. Its nature has been the subject of conflicting conjectures.
q: Thou shall put in the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Thummim.
And when Saul inquired of the Lord, the Lord answered him not, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets.

senses.d: The persons speaking, regarded as an object; ourselves; — the objective case of we. See We.
q: Give us this day our daily bread.

Us.etym: [OE. us, AS. �s; akin to OFries. & OS. �s, D. ons, G. uns, Icel. & Sw. oss, Dan. os, Goth. uns, L. nos we, us, Gr. � we, Skr. nas us. ����. Cf. Nostrum, Our.]

senses.d: The act of employing anything, or of applying it to one's service; the state of being so employed or applied; application; employment; conversion to some purpose; as, the use of a pen in writing; his machines are in general use.
q: Books can never teach the use of books.
This Davy serves you for good uses.
When he framed All things to man's delightful use.

senses.d: Occasion or need to employ; necessity; as, to have no further use for a book.
Yielding of service; advantage derived; capability of being used; usefulness; utility.
q: God made two great lights, great for their use To man.
'T is use alone that sanctifies expense.

senses.d: Continued or repeated practice; customary employment; usage; custom; manner; habit.
q: Let later age that noble use envy.
How weary, stale, flat and unprofitable, Seem to me all the uses of this world!

senses.d: Common occurrence; ordinary experience.
q: O Cæsar! these things are beyond all use.

senses.d: The special form of ritual adopted for use in any diocese; as, the Sarum, or Canterbury, use; the Hereford use; the York use; the Roman use; etc.
q: From henceforth all the whole realm shall have but one use.

senses.d: The premium paid for the possession and employment of borrowed money; interest; usury.
q: Thou art more obliged to pay duty and tribute, use and principal, to him.

senses.d: The benefit or profit of lands and tenements. Use imports a trust and confidence reposed in a man for the holding of lands. He to whose use or benefit the trust is intended shall enjoy the profits. An estate is granted and limited to A for the use of B.
A stab of iron welded to the side of a forging, as a shaft, near the end, and afterward drawn down, by hammering, so as to lengthen the forging.

Use.etym: [OE. us use, usage, L. usus, from uti, p. p. usus, to use. See Use, v. t.]

senses.d: To make use of; to convert to one's service; to avail one's self of; to employ; to put a purpose; as, to use a plow; to use a chair; to use time; to use flour for food; to use water for irrigation.
q: Launcelot Gobbo, use your legs.
Some other means I have which may be used.

senses.d: To behave toward; to act with regard to; to treat; as, to use a beast cruelly.
q: How wouldst thou use me now?
Cato has used me ill.

senses.d: To practice customarily; to make a practice of; as, to use diligence in business.
q: Use hospitality one to another.

senses.d: To accustom; to habituate; to render familiar by practice; to inure; — employed chiefly in the passive participle; as, men used to cold and hunger; soldiers used to hardships and danger.
q: I am so used in the fire to blow.
Thou with thy compeers, Used to the yoke, draw'st his triumphant wheels.
I would, my son, that thou wouldst use the power Which thy discretion gives thee, to control And manage all.
To study nature will thy time employ: Knowledge and innocence are perfect joy.

Use.etym: [OE. usen, F. user to use, use up, wear out, LL. usare to use, from L. uti, p. p. usus, to use, OL. oeti, oesus; of uncertain origin. Cf. Utility.]

senses.d: To be wont or accustomed; to be in the habit or practice; as, he used to ride daily; — now disused in the present tense, perhaps because of the similarity in sound, between “use to,” and “used to.”
q: They use to place him that shall be their captain on a stone.
Fears use to be represented in an imaginary.
Thus we use to say, it is the room that smokes, when indeed it is the fire in the room.
Now Moses used to take the tent and to pitch it without the camp.

senses.d: To be accustomed to go; to frequent; to inhabit; to dwell; — sometimes followed by of.
q: He useth every day to a merchant's house.
Ye valleys low, where the mild whispers use Of shades, and wanton winds, and gushing brooks.

senses.d: To practice usury; to charge unlawful interest.
q: I usured not ne to me usured any man.

senses.d: Usury.
q: Foul usure and lucre of villainy.

senses.d: One who lends money and takes interest for it; a money lender.
q: If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as a usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury.

senses.d: One who lends money at a rate of interest beyond that established by law; one who exacts an exorbitant rate of interest for the use of money.
q: He was wont to call me usurer.

Usurer.etym: [F. usurier, LL. usurarius. See Usury, and cf. Usurarious.]

senses.d: To seize, and hold in possession, by force, or without right; as, to usurp a throne; to usurp the prerogatives of the crown; to usurp power; to usurp the right of a patron is to oust or dispossess him.
q: Alack, thou dost usurp authority.
Another revolution, to get rid of this illegitimate and usurped government, would of course be perfectly justifiable.

Usurp.etym: [L. usurpare, usurpatum, to make use of, enjoy, get possession of, usurp; the first part of usurpare is akin to usus use (see Use, n.): cf. F. usurper.]

senses.d: To commit forcible seizure of place, power, functions, or the like, without right; to commit unjust encroachments; to be, or act as, a usurper.
q: The parish churches on which the Presbyterians and fanatics had usurped.
And now the Spirits of the Mind Are busy with poor Peter Bell; Upon the rights of visual sense Usurping, with a prevalence More terrible than magic spell.

senses.d: A premium or increase paid, or stipulated to be paid, for a loan, as of money; interest.
q: Thou shalt not lend upon usury to thy brother; usury of money, usury of victuals, usury of anything that is lent upon usury.
Thou oughtest therefore to have put my money to the exchanges, and then at my coming I should have received mine own with usury.
What he borrows from the ancients, he repays with usury of ��is own.

senses.d: The practice of taking interest.
q: Usury . . . bringeth the treasure of a realm or state into a few ��nds.

senses.d: Interest in excess of a legal rate charged to a borrower for the use of money.

Usury.etym: [OE. usurie, usure, F. usure, L. usura use, usury, interest, fr. uti, p. p. usus, to use. See Use, v. t.]

senses.d: The first note in Guido's musical scale, now usually superseded by do. See Solmization.
Situated at the farthest point or extremity; farthest out; most distant; extreme; as, the utmost limits of the land; the utmost extent of human knowledge.
q: We coasted within two leagues of Antibes, which is the utmost town in France.
Betwixt two thieves I spend my utmost breath.

senses.d: Being in the greatest or highest degree, quantity, number, or the like; greatest; as, the utmost assiduity; the utmost harmony; the utmost misery or happiness.
q: He shall answer . . . to his utmost peril.
Six or seven thousand is their utmost power.

Utmost.etym: [OE. utmeste, utemest, AS. �temest, a superlative fr. �te out. ����. See Out, and cf. Aftermost, Outmost, Uttermost.]

senses.d: The most that can be; the farthest limit; the greatest power, degree, or effort; as, he has done his utmost; try your utmost.
q: We have tried the utmost of our friends.

senses.d: Outer.
q: As doth an hidden moth The inner garment fret, not th' utter touch.

senses.d: Situated on the outside, or extreme limit; remote from the center; outer.
q: Through utter and through middle darkness borne.
The very utter part of Saint Adelmes point is five miles from Sandwich.

senses.d: Complete; perfect; total; entire; absolute; as, utter ruin; utter darkness.
q: They . . . are utter strangers to all those anxious thoughts which disquiet mankind.

senses.d: Peremptory; unconditional; unqualified; final; as, an utter refusal or denial.

Utter.etym: [OE. utter, originally the same word as outer. See Out, and cf. Outer, Utmost.]

senses.d: To put forth or out; to reach out.
q: How bragly it begins to bud, And utter his tender head.

senses.d: To dispose of in trade; to sell or vend.
q: Such mortal drugs I have, but Mantua's law Is death to any he that utters them.
They bring it home, and utter it commonly by the name of Newfoundland fish.

senses.d: hence, to put in circulation, as money; to put off, as currency; to cause to pass in trade; — often used, specifically, of the issue of counterfeit notes or coins, forged or fraudulent documents, and the like; as, to utter coin or bank notes.
q: The whole kingdom should continue in a firm resolution never to receive or utter this fatal coin.

senses.d: To give public expression to; to disclose; to publish; to speak; to pronounce.
q: The words I utter Let none think flattery, for they 'll find 'em truth.
And the last words he uttered called me cruel.

Utter.syn: To deliver; give forth; issue; liberate; discharge; pronounce. See Deliver.
Utter.etym: [OE. outren, freq. of outen to utter, put out, AS. ūtian to put out, eject, fr. ūt out. √198. See Out, and cf. Utter, a.]

senses.d: The act of uttering.
Sale by offering to the public.
Putting in circulation; as, the utterance of false coin, or of forged notes.
Vocal expression; articulation; speech.
q: At length gave utterance to these words.

senses.d: Power or style of speaking; as, a good utterance.
q: They . . . began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.
O, how unlike To that large utterance of the early gods!

senses.d: The last extremity; the end; death; outrance.
q: Annibal forced those captives whom he had taken of our men to skirmish one against another to the utterance.

senses.d: In an utter manner; to the full extent; fully; totally; as, utterly ruined; it is utterly vain.
Extreme; utmost; being; in the farthest, greatest, or highest degree; as, the uttermost extent or end.

Uttermost.etym: [From Utter, a.; cf. Utmost, and Outermost.]

senses.d: The utmost; the highest or greatest degree; the farthest extent.
q: Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him.
He cannot have sufficient honor done unto him; but the uttermost we can do, we must.
